title: Three Hundred Men, Jars, and Torches
summary: God reduces Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred so that Israel cannot boast that its own strength saved it. To strengthen Gideon, God sends him into the Midianite camp by night, where he overhears a dream about a barley loaf flattening a tent. Gideon's three hundred surround the camp with horns, jars, and torches, the Midianites panic and turn on one another, and the tribes join in the pursuit, capturing and killing the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb.
story: Chapter 6 ended with Gideon still needing signs. Chapter 7 is the victory, and it is designed to leave no doubt about whose victory it is. God keeps shrinking the army until the outcome is impossible by human reckoning. It is the high point of Gideon's story and one of the most celebrated deliverances in Israel's memory; Isaiah later speaks of the day of Midian as a picture of God breaking an oppressor's rod (Isaiah 9:4). But the chapter's last verses, with Ephraim called in late, set up the tribal quarrels and the darker turn of chapter 8.
historical:
The battle takes place in the eastern Jezreel Valley. The spring of Harod lies at the foot of Mount Gilboa, on the south side of the valley, and the hill of Moreh rises on the north side, with the Midianite camp spread out between. After the rout, the fleeing army ran east and southeast toward the Jordan, past places such as Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah (later the hometown of Elisha, 1 Kings 19:16), aiming for the fords that would take them home to the desert. Gideon's call to Ephraim to seize the fords of the Jordan cut off that escape, much as Ehud's men had done against Moab (3:28).

Verse 3 mentions Mount Gilead, which is puzzling, since Gilead lies east of the Jordan while Gideon is camped west of it. Some scholars suggest a scribal slip for Gilboa, which is nearby; others think Gilead was the name of a local hill, or that the phrase is an idiom. The text doesn't resolve the question. Oreb and Zeeb, whose names mean raven and wolf, were remembered in later Israel (Psalm 83:11 and Isaiah 10:26).
cultural:
The release of the fearful (verse 3) follows the rule for Israel's army in Deuteronomy 20:8, which allowed any fearful man to go home so he would not make others lose heart. The night was divided into watches (in the Old Testament, usually three), and the middle watch began around ten at night. Striking just after the guard changed meant new sentries whose eyes had not adjusted and a sleeping camp.

Each man carried a ram's horn (the shofar, a signaling instrument) and a clay jar covering a torch. Normally only a few men in an army would carry horns to signal the troops, so three hundred horns sounding from every side would suggest an enormous force. Breaking the jars made a sudden crash and revealed three hundred lights in the dark. In the ancient world dreams were widely taken as messages from the gods, and a Midianite interpreting a dream for his friend was a familiar scene. Barley was the cheaper grain, the bread of poor farmers, while the tent represented the nomadic Midianites. The dream pictured a humble Israelite loaf overturning the raiders' camp.
literary: The chapter is built on reduction and reversal. The numbers fall from thirty-two thousand to ten thousand to three hundred. God explains the purpose at the start: lest Israel say, My own hand has saved me (verse 2). The test at the water (4 to 8) is deliberately obscure; the narrator doesn't explain why lapping mattered, which keeps the focus on God's choosing rather than on the men's merit. The scene in the enemy camp (9 to 15) answers Gideon's fear without being asked: God himself offers him a sign this time. The battle is described in terms of sound and light rather than combat; the only swords used are Midianite swords turned on one another (verse 22). The battle cry, A sword for the LORD and for Gideon, links God and his servant, though the ordering will matter in chapter 8, when Gideon begins to take more credit.

outline.t: Too many men: the fearful go home
The test at the water leaves three hundred
Gideon overhears the dream of the barley loaf
The night attack and Midian's panic
The tribes pursue, and Oreb and Zeeb are killed

doctrines.note: God deliberately makes the odds impossible so that the victory can only be his. Salvation belongs to the LORD, and he arranges events to make that plain.
Gideon's small army must trust God's word rather than their numbers. God also strengthens Gideon's faith through the overheard dream, meeting his fear before he asks.
The chapter shows a pattern of salvation found throughout Scripture: God rescues his people in a way that removes every ground for human boasting (verse 2).

words.note: Pa'ar, to glorify or boast oneself. God reduces the army lest Israel boast over him, claiming credit for the victory. The word goes to the root of the chapter: the danger is not only defeat but pride in victory.
Tsaraph, to refine or test, used of smelting metal to remove impurities. God says he will sift the army at the water. The image is of a refiner separating what he will use.
Chalom, dream. God uses a Midianite's dream and his friend's interpretation to encourage Gideon. The enemy camp itself announces its coming defeat.

Shophar, a ram's horn trumpet used to signal in war and in worship. Three hundred horns sounding together created the impression of a vast army. The horn recalls Jericho, where trumpets and a shout, not swords, brought the walls down (Joshua 6).

christ: The chapter shows God saving through weakness so that no one can boast, a pattern Paul applies to the gospel: God chose what is weak and lowly so that no one might boast before him, and Christ became our wisdom, righteousness, and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:27-31). Paul also speaks of having a treasure in jars of clay to show that the surpassing power belongs to God (2 Corinthians 4:7). Paul doesn't cite Gideon there, and his image is his own, but the resonance with lights hidden in clay jars is striking. The link is thematic. The deeper connection is that in the gospel, too, the victory comes from God rather than human strength, and comes in a form the world finds weak.

hard.q: What was the point of the test at the water, and were the lappers better soldiers?
hard.a: Interpreters have long disagreed. One view holds that the three hundred who lapped from their hands stayed alert, watching for danger, and were the more careful soldiers. Another view notes that the text never says this and that God's stated purpose was to reduce the army, not to find the best men. On this reading the test was essentially arbitrary, a way of sorting that highlighted God's choice. Some even suggest the lappers were the less disciplined group, making the point sharper. The text's own emphasis is on verse 2 and verse 7: God will save with the three hundred so that Israel cannot boast. Whatever the men's quality, the victory is presented as God's.

questions: God reduced Gideon's army so Israel could not boast. Where are you tempted to take credit for what God has done?
God offered Gideon a sign before he asked, knowing he was afraid. How has God met your fear in unexpected ways?
The three hundred had to trust that horns and jars would be enough. What small or strange act of obedience might God be asking of you?
